open-question.question: How do the three distribution repositories uHappyLogic/cairn-claude, uHappyLogic/cairn-antigravity, and uHappyLogic/cairn-codex come to stand as uHappyLogic/gurita-<host>, and what stands at each old name afterwards? Renamed in place, a repository keeps its releases, its traffic-data branch, and its secret, and GitHub redirects the old URL until something is created there, so an existing install's marketplace source still resolves and is served the renamed plugin; created fresh, it starts empty and the old repository remains to be kept, archived, or deleted. The two choices are asked together because what can stand at the old name depends on how the new repository came to exist. The source repository is not part of this question: it is renamed to uHappyLogic/gurita by decision.

Which version number does the release that publishes the rename carry? The last release is 1.9.0 and the release procedure requires only a bare MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH strictly greater than it. The release answers to the new names only, so an installed copy is installed again rather than updated, and it also carries the path-addressed redesign and the milestone-to-mission rename, each of which changes how every skill is invoked.
open-question.alternative: The release carries 2.0.0, a major bump over the last tag 1.9.0, chosen now and written into the release task, so `/release-plugin 2.0.0` passes the strictly-greater gate unchanged and the count continues in the renamed source repository beside its existing tags. The number itself says what the release is: answering to new names only, needing a reinstall rather than an update, and changing how every skill is invoked through the redesign and the word's rename, all of which a major version announces to anyone reading it, the distribution repositories' release lists and the CHANGELOG heading included, with no change to the release procedure. It departs from the project's own practice, which has never made a major bump since 1.0.1 and has shipped breaking changes as minor releases (1.7.0 retired an agent and changed an invocation path, 1.9.0 added a resolution flag every skill takes), so the version series stops being read by one rule; and the first Gurita release carries a 2 for history a new user of the new name never saw.

The release carries 1.10.0, the next minor version after 1.9.0, chosen now and written into the release task, continuing the 1.x series the way the project's earlier large releases (1.7.0, 1.8.0, 1.9.0) were numbered, with the release procedure unchanged. It keeps the version series under the one rule the project has actually followed, a minor bump for a significant change, breaking or not, and asks nothing new of the procedure or of readers of the CHANGELOG. The number understates the break: an installed copy cannot be updated to it and must be installed again under a new name with every invocation changed, and nothing in 1.10.0 warns a user or a version-pinning reader of that, so the whole warning rests on the notes and the documentation.

The release carries 1.0.0, treating Gurita as a new product whose count starts over, which rejects the premise that the number must exceed 1.9.0: the release procedure's strictly-greater gate is bypassed or amended for this one release, while the renamed source repository keeps its existing tags 0.9.0 through 1.9.0 (no tag 1.0.0 exists among them). It matches the user-facing fact that nothing upgrades in place: every install is a first install under a new name, so a first version for that name reads as honest as the rename, and the series a Gurita user sees starts with their own first release. It breaks the version gate the release procedure exists to enforce and leaves the source repository's tags non-monotone: 1.0.0 would sort below the 1.1.0–1.9.0 tags it follows, the next patch release 1.0.1 collides with an existing tag, and every release up to 1.9.x would need a gate exception or a tag clash, so the reset costs a procedure change now and confusion for the next several releases; how far this reaches also depends on how the distribution repositories come to stand under their new names, which a sibling question owns.

No version is decided in this mission: the release task states only that the release is published through `/release-plugin` at a version the maintainer supplies when it runs, any bare MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH the gate accepts, the choice postponed to release time rather than recorded as a decision now. It keeps the decision with the person who invokes the release anyway, at the moment every other change of the mission is in and the full extent of the break is visible, and spends no question-answering effort on a value the procedure's own gate already constrains. The mission converges with the number unrecorded, so derive-tasks writes a release task carrying an open choice that an unattended run cannot make and the notes and documentation cannot cite; whether that is workable depends on who runs the release, which a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: By what means does the release's CHANGELOG entry come to hold the rebranding notes the goal calls for? The release procedure composes the entry from the missions finished since the last tag, and it will find none: this mission is still live when it publishes as its own last task, and the work finished since 1.9.0 is read by no query. The procedure then takes its empty-range branch, condensing the commits since 1.9.0 into one "Changes since 1.9.0" section it asks the maintainer to accept, and its one pause before publishing lets the maintainer revise the committed entry.

How much upgrade guidance does the release's CHANGELOG entry carry for a user who holds an installed Cairn copy? By decision the notes are the rebranding, and everything else the release changed is described in the documentation rather than itemised. Not settled is whether the entry itself states the steps for moving an install to the new name on each host and the rule that live work is finished under the last Cairn release before upgrading, or only points to where the documentation states them.
open-question.alternative: The entry states the whole upgrade itself, beside the rebranding announcement: for each of the three hosts, the commands that take the old copy out and install the renamed one (on Claude Code removing the `cairn` marketplace and `cairn@cairn` and adding `uHappyLogic/gurita-claude` with `gurita@gurita`, plus re-enabling the new id where a project's settings enable the old one; on Antigravity removing `~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn` and extracting the archive into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita`; on Codex removing the old plugin and marketplace and adding `uHappyLogic/gurita-codex` with `gurita@gurita`), that invocations change from `cairn:` to `gurita:`, and, in full, the rule that every live milestone is finished with the copy it was started under (the last Cairn release) before upgrading, followed by one `/init-mission-base-workflow` run. It may still link the documentation, but needs nothing from it. The one text every upgrading user is shown, on the source release page and on each of the three distribution release pages that carry the same notes, is enough on its own to upgrade safely, so a user who reads only the release page neither leaves a stale Cairn copy beside the new one nor upgrades with a live milestone that the renamed plugin will never discover again. It is the longest entry and the furthest from the decision that the notes are the rebranding and everything else is in the documentation: the commands and the rule are typed a second time beside the README install sections and the `docs/workflow.md` upgrade paragraph, where the two can drift, and because a CHANGELOG entry is a release's notes verbatim and never revised, any host command that later changes stays wrong in it for good.

The entry states the two facts in a sentence or two each, with no commands: that the plugin must be installed again under its new name on every host (a reinstall, not an update, with no alias left for `cairn:`), and that live milestones are finished under the last Cairn release before upgrading. For the per-host commands and the full rule it links the places in the documentation that hold them, the README's install sections and the upgrade paragraph of `docs/workflow.md`, pinned to the release tag or to the default branch. The reader of the release page learns both things that can go wrong, the stale install and the stranded milestone, while every command and the rule's details keep their one home in the documentation, so the entry stays a short announcement in the spirit of the rebranding-only decision and has nothing in it that a later host change can make wrong. A user still has to follow a link to do anything, and the pointer is only as good as what it lands on: today no document states the steps for moving an install from the old name to the new one on each host (the Claude Code README's migration section describes switching marketplaces under an unchanged `cairn@cairn`), so this depends on what the READMEs say to a reader who knows the plugin as Cairn, an axis the sibling question on the former name in the READMEs owns.

The entry announces the rebranding and carries one sentence pointing an existing user to where the documentation states how to upgrade (the README's install sections and the upgrade paragraph of `docs/workflow.md`), stating neither the reinstall steps nor the rule that live milestones are finished first. It holds most closely to the recorded decision that the notes are the rebranding and everything else is described in the documentation, gives the shortest entry, and keeps a single source for every upgrade instruction. The one consequence that cannot be undone after the fact, upgrading with a live milestone that the renamed plugin neither discovers nor reads back, is visible only to a user who follows the link, and the link lands on guidance for moving an install only if the documentation is given it, which rests on the sibling question on the former name in the READMEs.

The entry is the rebranding announcement alone, as the release's notes usually are, with no upgrade steps, no statement of the finish-first rule, and no pointer to them; an existing user finds the new install commands in the README and the upgrade rule in `docs/workflow.md` unaided. The shortest entry and the most literal reading of the decision that the notes are the rebranding, adding nothing to the CHANGELOG that is not the announcement itself. The release is a hard cut that answers to the new names only, so every existing user must reinstall and must finish live work first, yet the one text all of them see on upgrading tells them neither nor where to look, leaving a stranded milestone or a stale `cairn` copy as the likely result for anyone who upgrades straight from the release page.

open-question.question: What do the root README and the three host READMEs tell a reader who knows the plugin as Cairn? A link to the source repository's old URL lands on the renamed README, which after a plain substitution would say nothing of the former name, and the Claude Code host README carries a "Migrating from the old marketplace" section stating that installs from uHappyLogic/cairn keep working and updating under the unchanged id cairn@cairn, which no longer holds once the marketplace and the plugin are named gurita. A reader who knows the plugin as Cairn finds the connection only in the release's CHANGELOG entry and the documentation, never on a README. The hard cut applies to prose as fully as to identifiers. The READMEs describe only the plugin as it now stands, and there is no old-name text for a later whole-tree search to list as residue or for a later release to retire. A reader following a link to uHappyLogic/cairn, which by decision redirects to the renamed source repository, lands on a page that never says it is the plugin they knew. An existing Claude Code user loses the only install-migration text in the tree, and no README tells them that their cairn@cairn install no longer updates.

The root README carries one sentence near its title and pitch saying that Gurita was published as Cairn up to 1.9.0 and that the old names no longer work, with a link to where the upgrade steps are documented. The three host README templates are a plain substitution with no mention of the former name, and the Claude Code host README's migration section and its lead-in line are removed. The one page that old links are guaranteed to reach, the redirected source repository's landing page, acknowledges the old name, at the cost of a single sentence. The install-facing host READMEs stay free of it. A user reading a distribution repository's README, which is the page an existing install's marketplace source points at, sees no word of the former name. Whether that page is ever reached through an old URL depends on how the distribution repositories reach their new names. The linked steps must also exist somewhere in the docs, which they may not yet do for each host.

The same one-sentence former-name note stands in the root README and in each of the three host README templates, so it renders into every host tree. Each note says Gurita was published as Cairn up to 1.9.0, that the old names no longer work, and links to where the upgrade steps are documented. The Claude Code host README's "Migrating from the old marketplace" section is removed, and the note stands in its place. No README carries upgrade steps of its own. Wherever a Cairn user lands, the source repository or any distribution repository, the page says it is the same plugin under a new name, worded the same way on every host. Four files carry the old name for good, and the rename's completeness bar has to list it as residue in the root and in three templates. The note tells a user that their install has stopped updating but not how to move it, so the user still has to look elsewhere for steps that may not yet be written per host.

The root README carries a short "Coming from Cairn" section. It lists the names that changed: the plugin and marketplace id, the skill and agent namespace and its invocation forms, the repositories, and the Antigravity install path. It states the rule that live work is finished under the last Cairn release before upgrading, and gives each host's commands for removing the old install and installing the new one. Each host README template carries one line naming the former name and linking to that section. The Claude Code host README's old migration section is removed. One complete upgrade path stands in one place, on the page the old URL lands on, with each host's steps written once rather than spread across three templates. It places the largest standing old-name surface on the landing page of a plugin whose low adoption is the stated ground for the hard cut. It restates upgrade guidance that the release's CHANGELOG entry and the docs may also carry, so the three must be kept in step. Readers of a host README take one more hop to reach their own commands.

Each host README template carries a "Migrating from Cairn" section with its own host's steps, placed beside that host's install commands. In the Claude Code README the existing section is rewritten: remove the cairn marketplace, add uHappyLogic/gurita-claude, install gurita@gurita, and change /cairn: invocations to /gurita:. The Antigravity section moves ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn to the gurita path. The Codex section covers the marketplace, the plugin id, and the $gurita: form. Each section also states the rule that live work is finished under the last Cairn release first. The root README carries one sentence naming the former name and pointing to each host's install section. The steps sit next to the install commands they replace, in the README of the repository the user actually installed from. The Claude Code README's existing migration text is corrected rather than dropped. Three sections have to be written and kept accurate, and each one's commands are confirmed only by trying them on that host. The old name renders into every host tree. What each section can say about the old source, whether it still resolves or stands empty, depends on how the distribution repositories reach their new names.

The root README carries the full "Coming from Cairn" section: the changed names, the finish-first rule, and every host's commands. Each host README template also carries its own complete "Migrating from Cairn" section with that host's steps, the Claude Code README's existing section among them, rewritten to the new names. Every README is self-contained for a Cairn user, and none depends on a link to another. Whichever README a Cairn user reaches, it gives them everything they need to move their install, with no hop and no dependence on the docs. The same steps are written twice for each host, in the root README and in that host's template, and kept in step with each other and with the release's CHANGELOG entry. This is the largest standing old-name surface of any option, carried for good across four files.

open-question.question: What shows that the old name is gone from everywhere it should be, and over which surface? The drift gate and both test runs pin behaviour, not the name, and no build check bans or requires it, so a leftover cairn in runtime prose, a host template, a slot value, or the docs fails nothing. The milestone-to-mission rename used two bars: a permanent build check over core/ with a short list of allowed forms, and one closing whole-tree search compared by hand against a recorded list of what stays. Completeness is shown once, by one closing task whose verified bar records a whole-tree search over every tracked file, `hosts/`, `uv.lock`, and file paths included (`git grep -I -i cairn` beside `git ls-files | grep -i cairn`), every hit compared by hand against a residue list of what stays, each residue entry naming its file, count, and the decision that keeps it, as the word's rename recorded in its `Whole-Tree Search Against the Residue` bar. Proves completeness only at one commit: a leftover written later, for instance a copied old install command in a new slot value or template, fails nothing, and the hand comparison against the residue list is judgment a runner can get wrong; what the list holds depends on the siblings that settle past CHANGELOG entries, the former name in the READMEs, the hands-on check blocks, and the plugin-named file names.

The word's-rename precedent carried over as it stood: a permanent build check over `core/` only, beside `host-name-in-core` and `old-word-in-core`, refusing `cairn` in any capitalisation in paths and lines with a short list of allowed forms (likely none, since core/ holds the name once, as prose), plus the same one closing whole-tree search against a residue list recorded in the closing task's bar. Follows the shape the project already used and reviewed for a rename, so the check, its docstring, and its failure messages are a copy of an existing pattern, and core/, the runtime layer every host renders, can never carry the old name again. The permanent part guards the one place the name barely stood: nearly every identifier site is in the host definitions under scripts/hosts/ and in the trees rendered from them, which the check never reads, so it adds code for almost no protection, and everything else rests on the one-time search as in the search-only option.

A permanent build check over the build's whole input set, `core/` and every host definition under `scripts/hosts/` (settings.toml values, slot value files, templates, and paths, such as the Codex template directory), refusing `cairn` in any capitalisation outside a short list of allowed forms; the rendered `hosts/` trees are covered through it, since they are pure build output that `--check` keeps equal to a fresh build. Plus the one closing whole-tree search against a residue list recorded in the closing task's bar, for the files outside the build (README, docs, CONTRIBUTING, .github, host_tests, the root marketplace, the tooling project, idea drafts). Puts the permanent guard exactly where the identifiers live, the marketplace names, plugin_root, the namespaced agent names in the three Claude Code slot values, and the Codex plugins/ path, so the drift gate in CI fails any later reintroduction in shipped runtime files, while the closing search covers the prose surface once. The build would scan host definitions for a word for the first time, a new kind of check beyond host-name-in-core's core-only scope, and its allowed-form list must carry whatever the hands-on check blocks keep (a sibling decides whether they keep the old names), and every future old-name mention in a host definition, even a deliberate one, needs a list edit.

The same permanent build check over `core/` and `scripts/hosts/`, with its allowed-form list, and no closing whole-tree search: the files outside the build (README, docs, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY.md, issue templates, host_tests, the root marketplace, pyproject.toml and uv.lock, .claude/, idea drafts) are shown renamed only by the verified bars of the tasks that rename them, each bar recording its own area's search. Every check that stands is mechanical and permanent, with no one-off hand comparison against a residue list, and each rename task already owes a bar that can carry its own area's search. Nothing ever looks at the whole tree at once, so a file no task was scoped to (a stray mention in a test, a workflow comment, a path such as docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md if no task owns it) is missed silently, which is the gap the word's rename closed with its last task.

A permanent pytest test over every tracked file and path (git ls-files and file contents, any capitalisation, hosts/ included), refusing `cairn` outside an allowlist kept in the test of the files and forms that stay (the CHANGELOG's entries, idea drafts, this mission's own files, whatever residue the siblings keep), run by both test runs in CI; it stands in for both the build check and the closing search, and the closing task's bar records that it passes. The only option where the whole surface, prose and identifiers alike, stays checked after the mission finishes, mechanically and in CI, so no later edit anywhere can reintroduce the old name unnoticed and no hand comparison is ever needed. A permanent, tree-wide allowlist is a hand-maintained list of exceptions that grows with every deliberate mention (history notes, a design draft citing the rename, release notes that name the former name), turns a test failure on for ordinary prose, and holds the old word in the test file itself; nothing comparable was kept for the word's rename, and what the allowlist must hold depends on the siblings deciding past CHANGELOG entries, the former name in the READMEs, and the hands-on check blocks.

Make the name structurally single-sourced instead of checked by word: every identifier site in the host definitions that now writes the name literally (both marketplace names, the Codex displayName, source path, plugin_dir, and layout paths, Antigravity's plugin_root, the namespaced agent names in the Claude Code slot values, the manifest descriptions) is rendered from `plugin_name` through a placeholder, and a permanent build check refuses the literal plugin name in any host definition, so changing `plugin_name` is the rename of every built identifier; plus the one closing whole-tree search against a residue list for the files outside the build. Verifies the identifier surface by construction rather than by search, and makes any later rename of the shipped identifiers a one-value change, the same reasoning that gave the principle store a name-free path. Requires changing the build and an invariant: slot values may carry no placeholder other than PLUGIN_ROOT, and the Codex template directory name and the Antigravity plugin root would need placeholder expansion in paths and settings, so the mission takes on build redesign beyond a rename, and the prose surface (README, docs) is still covered only by the one-time search.

No completeness bar of its own: no build check, no test, and no closing whole-tree search; each rename task's verified bar shows its own area renamed, and the drift gate and both test runs stay the only standing verification, unchanged. Adds no task, no check, and no residue list to maintain, and keeps the mission to the renames themselves, each already verified where it was made. Nothing shows the name gone from everywhere: the drift gate and the test runs pin behaviour, not the name, so a site no task named fails nothing, and the cross-area leftovers (a docs file citing an install path, a test identity, a .gitignore entry) are exactly what per-area bars miss.

open-question.question: Where, and at what length, does the README explain the name Gurita? The naming draft holds that the name says nothing to most English speakers and that its meaning, Indonesian for octopus with the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out on their own, should be one sentence away on the landing page. The README today explains no name: its "Why Cairn?" section is about handing long-running work to an agent, not about the word.

What happens to the .gitignore entry .cairn/daemon.toml? It is the file's first line and names a path under a directory called after the plugin, yet nothing else in the tree names that path, no tool creates it, and no such directory stands in the maintainer's checkout.
open-question.alternative: The `.gitignore` entry `.cairn/daemon.toml` stays exactly as it stands, as the file's first line, under the old name. The rename does not touch it, now or later: it is treated as a line about a local file outside the plugin's identifier sites, not as a place the plugin's name lands. Nothing is lost if some program on a maintainer's machine still writes `.cairn/daemon.toml` into the checkout: the entry was added by hand as the whole of the new `.gitignore` in `35ad784` ("milestone 10 prepared", 2026-07-14), no commit since has touched or explained it, and keeping it is the one choice that needs no answer about what wrote it. The old name stays in a tracked root file the goal says to rename everywhere, with no alias, so the closing check has to list it as a known leftover with a reason nobody can give. Whether that is allowed depends on the surface and bar the completeness question settles. It also keeps a line that, by every trace in the tree and its history, guards nothing.

The entry is rewritten to `.gurita/daemon.toml`, the same file name under a directory named after the new plugin name, still as the file's first line. It is changed like every other occurrence of the name, by substitution. The rename stays mechanical and the bar stays simple: every `cairn` becomes `gurita` with no case judged one by one, and the ignore rule keeps its shape for a daemon config that would be expected, by analogy, under the new name. It protects a path nothing creates. No tool in the tree or anything recorded writes `.gurita/daemon.toml`, so the line goes from guarding an unexplained file to guarding one that cannot exist. A program that really did write `.cairn/daemon.toml` would lose its ignore rule without anyone noticing.

The `.cairn/daemon.toml` line is deleted from `.gitignore`, under neither name, and nothing replaces it. The other six entries stay as they are, `.scratchpad.md` becoming the first line. It drops a dead entry along with the old name. Nothing in the tree or its history names the path, no tool creates it, and no `.cairn/` directory stands in the checkout, so the tree ends up with no leftover to explain and no made-up new path to protect. If some program outside the repository (a local daemon or an older tool the maintainer once ran) still writes `.cairn/daemon.toml` into a checkout, that file shows as untracked and could be committed by a careless `git add`. Its origin was never recorded, so the risk can only be judged, not checked.

The line is taken out of the tracked `.gitignore`, and the maintainer keeps the rule `.cairn/daemon.toml` in an untracked ignore file of their own, either the checkout's `.git/info/exclude` or their global git excludes file. The repository then names the path nowhere. The old name leaves the tracked tree as the goal asks, and any stray file a program on the maintainer's machine might still write stays ignored there, which matches what the entry seems to be: a local machine's concern, added by hand, that no contributor's checkout shares. It writes outside the tracked tree into the maintainer's own git configuration, where no commit records it and no other clone gets it. It is a second place to keep up for a rule whose need nobody has confirmed, and it does nothing for any other contributor whose machine might write the same file.
